Why Standard Waiting Rooms Are Helping Scalper Bots Win

Share

Twitter
Linkedin
Email
WhatsApp
Telegram
    B2BNN Newsdesk
    August 27, 2026

    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 4:09
    Instaread

    A virtual waiting room looks fair at first glance. Everyone gets a place, everyone waits, and access opens as capacity becomes available – just like a regular queue at the grocery store or DMV. Yet, online, that system has a weakness during major ticket releases: parts of your traffic will be genuine, human buyers, whereas other parts of your traffic will be bots.

    That’s a serious problem when tickets for a popular concert or sporting event sell quickly. Keeping a website online isn’t much consolation if real customers spend 45 minutes waiting behind automated scalping operations.

    The Flaw in Traditional Queues

    Basic virtual queues are designed around traffic control. Too many visitors arrive, so some are held back and admitted gradually. The model works when everyone in line deserves to be there.

    Scalper bots complicate matters because automated systems can make requests at a scale an individual customer can’t match. If the waiting room doesn’t identify those requests, bots may secure queue positions before many genuine buyers have even joined.

    The queue hasn’t technically failed. It’s doing exactly what it was designed to do. The problem is that traffic management and customer verification are different jobs.

    The “Dormant Bot” Trap

    It’s tempting to imagine ticket bots constantly hammering a website with requests. Modern automation can be considerably less obvious. A bot can enter a queue and wait without immediately doing anything that attracts attention. Once it reaches the ticketing site, its behavior may change as it begins targeting inventory or making requests through available endpoints.

    That creates a weakness for waiting rooms that assess visitors only once. The visitor that looked acceptable when joining the line isn’t necessarily behaving the same way 20 minutes later. By the time suspicious activity becomes obvious at checkout, genuine customers may already have spent their time waiting behind it.

    The Natural Pivot

    This is where a different approach becomes useful. DataDome is a cybersecurity company that helps businesses identify and block malicious bots, automated agents and online fraud across websites, mobile applications and APIs.

    For high-demand releases, it applies that security expertise to virtual queuing. Its waiting room technology analyzes traffic before visitors are admitted, allowing unwanted automation to be filtered rather than simply assigned a number in line.

    For ticketing businesses trying to stop scalper bots, the important difference is where the security check happens. Bot detection becomes part of managing access to the sale rather than something left until the purchase process is already underway.

    One Check Isn’t Enough

    Filtering traffic before the queue is useful, but it doesn’t solve everything. Automation can adapt during a session, which makes continued assessment important.

    DataDome’s approach includes evaluating activity throughout the waiting period. If behavior later indicates unwanted automation, that session can be addressed rather than keeping its place simply because it passed an earlier check.

    Genuine visitors can still move through an orderly queue. The difference is that the system isn’t assuming every session remains trustworthy from arrival to checkout. That matters when inventory is limited. Every bot occupying a queue position can represent another genuine buyer waiting unnecessarily.

    The Customer Experience Matters Too

    Ticket sellers can’t solve the scalping problem by making every visitor complete endless security checks. A customer who has waited for a major release already has limited patience. Adding unnecessary challenges creates another source of frustration.

    The better approach is to identify suspicious automation in the background wherever possible and reserve additional checks for cases that actually warrant them. Security then supports the queue instead of becoming another obstacle inside it.

    Final Thoughts

    Traditional waiting rooms solve an important technical problem, but keeping a ticketing website available doesn’t automatically make access fair. Scalper bots exploit the gap between managing traffic and understanding who is generating it. Once automated buyers receive ordinary queue positions, genuine fans can end up waiting behind them.

    DataDome tackles that gap by bringing bot detection into the queue itself and continuing to assess sessions during the wait. The result is a different idea of queue management: don’t just organize everyone who arrives. Work out who belongs in the line first.
